summary: Discovery with Zephyrus on suitability of Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a regulated, multi-region inference product. Main concerns: predictable latency under failover, auditability (audit logs/KMS), regional routing and cost tradeoffs; agree to run a 3-region pilot and deeper SE-led benchmarks.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private fit
transcript:
Header: 2026-09-21 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~54m | Recording: auto
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO), Liam (SRE Lead), Sofia (Product), Evan (Security)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the infra team. With me is Diego, our systems SE.
[00:07] Priya (Zephyrus): Hi Maya, hi Diego. Thanks. We wanted to validate assumptions around fallback behavior and private deployment suitability before we budget for Dedicated.
[00:15] Diego (Redwood): Totally. High level we want to understand your failure modes and then map to our routing/fallback knobs — model variants, regional steering, and fallthrough to lower-cost instances.
[00:25] Liam (Zephyrus SRE): To be upfront — we have hard SLAs for our agents: 99.7% p95 under normal conditions, but during region outage we accept increased p95 to 750-800ms for non-critical requests. Critical paths must stay under 300ms.
[00:40] Sofia (Product): And we need deterministic behavior for the payment flow and the recommendation path — they have different tolerances.
[00:48] Diego: Got it. Quick question: are you looking to run anything on-prem, or is this cloud-only?
[00:52] Priya: We're evaluating three options: Redwood Hosted to move fast, Dedicated for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC or on-prem) for our regulated EU and APAC customers. If we go Dedicated we want dedicated GPU pools with a commit.
[01:05] Evan (Security): From compliance side, we need audit logs, KMS integration, and the ability to certify keys for EU data residency. Also SOC 2 docs.
[01:12] Maya: We can provide SOC 2 and detailed audit log examples. For Private we have a customer-controlled control plane option so keys can be customer-managed HSM/KMS. I'll share that pack after this call.
[01:22] Priya: Great. On failover — what does your multi-region steering look like? We need both active-active for low-latency routes and active-passive for some EU-only workloads.
[01:31] Diego: We support policy-driven routing. Typical pattern: prefer local region, route to nearest fallback region, and optionally degrade to a smaller model variant or lower quantization. There's also automatic fallback to a warm standby for Dedicated customers.
[01:42] Liam: Warm standby meaning what exactly? Are we talking kept-up GPUs or cold containers?
[01:47] Diego: For Dedicated, warm standby is reserved idle capacity — GPUs booted and session hot; for Hosted we do fast spin-ups but with higher latency hit. For Private, you can configure similar keep-warm pools if your infra permits it.
[01:58] Priya: And how do you handle KV cache warmness across regions? We can't have cold-start penalties when routing.
[02:04] Diego: There is prefix/KV cache replication options — it's not fully synchronous by default, that can be tuned. I should note sometimes the transcripting swaps KG cache — it's key/value cache — sorry, small note.
[02:15] Sofia: So if a EU region fails and traffic goes to NA, we want no more than 200ms add on for token generation. Is that realistic?
[02:24] Diego: That depends: model size, sequence length, and quantization. For smaller models and short sequences, <200ms is feasible across regions for streaming outputs; larger gen or long context will be higher. We need to benchmark your exact prompts.
[02:36] Priya: Understood. Let's talk SLOs. Do you offer formal SLAs that map to credits for uptime and latency?
[02:43] Maya: For Hosted we have published SLAs for availability; Dedicated comes with contractual latency/throughput SLOs depending on the capacity tier and commitment. Private deployments are via enterprise contract with tailored SLAs.
[02:55] Evan: For audit purposes, we need request-level tracing and token-level cost attribution so finance can reconcile usage.
[03:03] Maya: Console has token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards; we can demo that in the follow-up.
[03:09] Liam: A lot of our concern is graceful degradation strategy. If a region gets slow due to network flaps, we don't want to bulk-reroute everything instantly. Throttle, circuit-breaker, some de-prioritization.
[03:19] Diego: Exactly. We provide circuit-breakers and can configure progressive traffic shifting — e.g., route 5% to fallback, monitor error/latency, then increase. Canary style. Also tail latency isolation via queue shaping.
[03:31] Priya: That sounds good. What about consistency for KV cache? If we do canary traffic split, we want the same prefix caches to be warmed.
[03:40] Diego: You can pin prefixes to a region or use cross-region replication. Tradeoffs: replication adds cross-region bandwidth and eventual consistency.
[03:49] Sofia: Cost-wise what are the levers? We saw guidance about batching and quantization suggestions.
[03:55] Maya: Redwood Optimize will recommend batching and quantization profiles by workload; for Dedicated you'll also control reserved pool sizing and burst policies. That balances cost vs latency.
[04:05] Priya: In the event of a partial outage we need route fallback plus model fallback. Can Redwood do both automatically?
[04:11] Diego: Yes — routing policy can cascade to model variants. E.g., primary: large fp16 in eu-west, fallback: quantized int8 in eu-west fallback region, fallback 2: hosted small-mem model. You can configure quality thresholds to trigger a switch.
[04:25] Liam: How are rollbacks handled if a fallback model has a subtle quality regression? We need evals and quick rollback with traffic split.
[04:32] Diego: We integrate with evals and have automatic regression alerts tied to prompt sets. You can auto-roll back on a quality drop signal. We recommend canary for any new model or fallback config.
[04:44] Maya: For pilot scope, we're proposing a 3-region pilot: EU(Frankfurt) primary, fallback to UK and US-WEST, with a Dedicated pool for EU traffic and Hosted fallback. That lets you test both Dedicated guarantees and Hosted fallback economics.
[04:58] Priya: EU-->UK-->US-WEST, ok. For data residency — some EU customers require that inference never leaves EU. How do we enforce that?
[05:06] Diego: You can enforce region constraints via routing policy and hard block for certain tenants. For those we recommend Private deployment in EU region or Dedicated with strict routing plus contractual constraints.
[05:16] Evan: Can keys be kept in our KMS so Redwood never sees plaintext model inputs?
[05:20] Maya: For Private we can do customer-managed KMS/HSM and the control plane is customer-controlled. For Dedicated there's a managed option or customer keys via KMS integration. We'll provide the specifics in the security doc.
[05:31] Priya: Latency SLOs asymmetric by flow — payment path must hit <300ms and we need 99.9% for that. Is that something Redwood can contractually commit to?
[05:40] Maya: For Dedicated yes, depending on commit level and topology. We'll need to size the dedicated pool and agree on traffic shaping. We should model the worst-case bursts.
[05:48] Liam: What about chaos testing and simulating region outages? Can Redwood accommodate that during pilot?
[05:53] Diego: Absolutely. We can run chaos windows where we simulate region loss and measure failover times and error budgets. That would be part of the SE-led deep-dive.
[06:03] Sofia: Ok, let's talk timeline — we want a pilot starting in October, two weeks duration, with a follow-on evaluation meeting.
[06:09] Maya: Sounds doable. Diego and I will draft a pilot plan with metrics, acceptance criteria, and runbook.
[06:14] Priya: Acceptance criteria: failover < 30s for traffic steering, token-level cost delta <25% during fallback for recommendation path, and critical payment path latency <300ms at 99.9% during failover.
[06:27] Diego: We'll put those into the pilot SLA. Quick note — some customers we've worked with require private-deploy for regulated customers, but they still want Redwood Console for observability. Our private control plane supports that.
[06:38] Evan: How about SSO and role-based access? We need SAML integration and fine-grained RBAC.
[06:43] Maya: Yes SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported. For Private we can map to your AD/IdP.
[06:48] Liam: On logging — do you provide immutable audit logs for compliance? We need append-only logs for requests and admin changes.
[06:55] Diego: We provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM. For Private deployments, logs can be routed to your storage and we support write-once config for retention.
[07:04] Priya: Cool. What about cost transparency during failover? We don't want surprise billing if fallback sends traffic to a more expensive region.
[07:11] Maya: Console shows token-level and regional cost attribution. For Dedicated, we can set routing policies that limit cross-region failover beyond a certain budget threshold.
[07:21] Sofia: Any limitations on model types in Private? We have some custom fine-tuned checkpoints.
[07:27] Diego: Private supports customer model onboarding with the usual validation and kernel selection process. Large fine-tunes may need additional quantization passes.
[07:36] Priya: Ok. I have one last question: for the canary progressive ramp you mentioned, what's a safe ramp schedule you recommend?
[07:42] Diego: Typical: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with 10–15 minute observation windows, but with region failover we might shorten windows and use latency/error rate thresholds as gates.
[07:54] Maya: Great. Any other immediate blockers?
[07:58] Priya: Budget — we need a ballpark for Dedicated reserve cost and expected Hosted fallback bill for our projected Q4 traffic.
[08:05] Maya: I'll send draft pricing — we'll include committed capacity options and a fallback-hosted burn rate projection.
[08:12] (small crosstalk) Liam: Also can we get a short example runbook for incident response?
[08:17] Diego: Yes, will include typical runbook steps, rollback, and telemetry checks.
[08:22] Maya: Ok recap: Redwood to send SOC2, private deploy checklist, and pricing. SE to prepare pilot test plan and benchmark runbook. Zephyrus to share traffic matrix and compliance regions. We'll schedule a 2h SE deep-dive next week.
[08:37] Priya: That works. Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.
[08:42] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., KV cache transcribed as KG cache), filler words present, some speaker overlap.
